V: Renal or bladder calculi with mucosal irritation/hematuria: stones can cause dysuria, suprapubic pain and microscopic/macroscopic hematuria
I: Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis: classic triad of dysuria, suprapubic pain and malodorous urine ± hematuria
Urethritis (Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea): dysuria and minimal hematuria without marked systemic illness
N: Early bladder carcinoma: can first manifest with painless hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms
D: Interstitial cystitis (painful bladder syndrome): chronic pelvic pain worsened by bladder filling, but usually long-standing not 6-day onset
I2: Medication-induced hematuria (anticoagulants, cyclophosphamide) – no such drugs reported
C: Congenital urinary tract anomaly predisposing to infection (e.g., vesicoureteral reflux) – no history
A: Autoimmune cystitis (e.g., lupus cystitis) – rare, typically systemic features absent
T: Urethral/bladder trauma (e.g., recent instrumentation, sexual trauma) – patient denies precipitating events
E: Metabolic nephrolithiasis (hypercalciuria, uric acid) – stone possibility covered under V

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic presentation in young-middle-aged woman: 6-day acute dysuria, foul-smelling urine, suprapubic pain, mild hematuria, absence of systemic or flank symptoms.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Urethritis due to sexually transmitted infection (Chlamydia/Gonorrhoea)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dysuria with minimal hematuria can be urethral inflammation; absence of vaginal discharge does not exclude; sexual history limited.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Urinary tract calculi (bladder or distal ureteric stone)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Stones can produce dysuria, suprapubic pain and hematuria; pain often colicky and may radiate; no flank pain lowers probability.
Produces suprapubic pain and dysuria but classically chronic, not acute onset, and usually sterile urine.
Hematuria and irritative voiding possible but age <50, acute onset, and foul odour favour infection.
